measures.questionText: To improve the quality of education; repair or replace leaky roofs; modernize/renovate outdated classrooms, restrooms and school facilities; and replace deteriorating plumbing and sewer systems; shall Winters Joint Unified School District’s measure authorizing $29,900,000 in bonds, at legal interest rates, and levying approximately $49 per $100,000 of assessed valuation (raising $1,600,000 annually) while bonds are outstanding, be adopted, with a Board-appointed citizens’ oversight committee and annual independent audits to assure proper expenditure of funds?
measures.officialStatement:
WINTERS JOINT UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT SCHOOL BONDS — MEASURE B
IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS BY YOLO COUNTY COUNSEL

This measure was placed on the ballot by the Board of Trustees of the Winters Joint Unified School
District, which lies within Yolo and Solano Counties. If approved, it would authorize the District to issue
and sell general obligation bonds in an amount not to exceed $29,900,000.

Under the California Constitution (Article XII A and Article XVI) and Education Code section 15266, a
school district may issue general obligation bonds for the construction, reconstruction, rehabilitation, or
replacement of school facilities, including furnishing and equipping them and acquiring or leasing real
property, upon approval of 55% of the voters voting on the measure, The bonds would be repaid, with
interest, from an ad valorem tax levied on taxable property within the District, in proportion to each
property's assessed value.

Proceeds could be used only for the school facilities projects identified in the measure's Bond Project List.
These include repairing or replacing leaky roofs, deteriorating plumbing, sewer systems, and outdated
heating and air conditioning; modernizing or renovating classrooms, restrooms, and school facilities;
making health, safety, accessibility (including ADA), and security improvements; upgrading technology,
electrical wiring, athletic fields, parking, and grounds; improving energy efficiency; abating hazardous
materials; and acquiring real property for school facilities. By law, bond proceeds may not be used for
teacher or administrator salaries, pensions, or other school operating expenses.

The measure includes accountability provisions required by law: proceeds must be deposited in a separate
account; an independent citizens' oversight committee must be appointed; and the District must conduct
annual independent performance and financial audits until the funds are spent, along with an annual report
to the Board of Trustees.

The District's Tax Rate Statement estimates the average annual tax rate required to fund the bonds at
$46.00 per $100,000 of assessed valuation, and the highest tax rate at $49.00 per $100,000 of assessed
valuation, first occurring in fiscal year 2027-28, The final fiscal year the tax is anticipated to be collected
is 2061-62, The best estimate of the total debt service (principal and interest) if all bonds are issued and
sold is $58,600,000. These estimates are based on the District's projections and are not binding; actual
rates and amounts may vary. The tax is based on a property's assessed value, not its market value.

This measure requires approval by 55% of the voters voting on it.

A"YES" vote is a vote to authorize the District to issue up to $29,900,000 in general obligation bonds
and to levy the property tax necessary to repay them.

A"NO" vote is a vote against authorizing the bonds and the associated property tax.

Dated: July 13, 2026

CEDRIC HOES SENIOR DERU vy

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure B. If you desire a copy of the Measure,
please call the Yolo County Registrar of Voters at (530) 666-8133 or (800) 649-9943 and a copy will
be mailed at no cost to you. The full text of the Measure may also be viewed online at:

http://www. yoloelections.org/.

measures.officialStatement:
COUNTY COUNSEL’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE E

MEASURE E — SOLANO COUNTY UNINCORPORATED BUSINESS LICENSE TAX

Measure E would amend Article XII of Chapter 11 of the Solano County Code to increase the
business license tax on commercial wind turbine generators and impose business license taxes
on commercial solar energy systems, front-of-the-meter battery energy storage systems, natural
gas extraction facilities, and data centers in the unincorporated areas of Solano County.

Measure E would:

   •   Increase the commercial wind turbine tax rate from $0.00003 to $0.00008 per kilowatt-
       hour;

   •   Impose a tax of $0.00008 per kilowatt-hour on electricity generated by commercial solar
       energy systems;

   •   Impose a monthly capacity-based tax of $1.50 per megawatt-hour of approved energy
       storage capacity on front-of-the-meter battery energy storage systems, regardless of
       actual charging or discharging;

   •   Impose a tax of $0.30 per thousand cubic feet of natural gas extracted; and

   •   Impose an annual tax of $5.00 per square foot of gross floor area on data centers,
       including equipment-pad areas associated with ancillary behind-the-meter battery
       energy storage systems and natural gas turbines supporting a data center. The tax
       would not apply to information technology infrastructure that is accessory to and
       primarily supports specified on-site uses.

Beginning January 1, 2028, the tax rates would be adjusted annually based on changes in the
Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers but could not decrease. The Director of
Resource Management would calculate and publish the adjusted rates. Persons or entities
exempt from business license taxes under federal or state law would remain exempt.

Revenues would be deposited into the County General Fund and could be used for any lawful
governmental purpose. County staff estimate the measure would generate approximately
$353,000 in additional annual revenue.

Measure E is a general tax and requires approval by a majority of voters voting on the measure.
If approved, it would take effect January 1, 2027. The measure does not contain an expiration
date.

A "yes" vote is a vote to approve the proposed amendments to the County's Business License
Tax.

A "no" vote is a vote to retain the current Business License Tax provisions, including the existing
commercial wind turbine tax rate, without the proposed tax categories or annual inflation
adjustments.

measures.questionText: To fund local programs and essential public services, shall Solano County increase its existing Transient Occupancy Tax, paid by tourists and others staying overnight at short-term lodging facilities in unincorporated areas (excluding cities), from 5% to 12% of the total rent charged, providing approximately an additional $58,500 annually, until ended by the voters?
measures.officialStatement:
COUNTY COUNSEL’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE H
           MEASURE H - – SOLANO COUNTY UNINCORPORATED TRANSIENT
                             OCCUPANCY TAX


Measure H would amend Article II of Chapter 11 of the Solano County Code to increase
the County's Transient Occupancy Tax ("TOT") within the unincorporated areas of
Solano County from 5% to 12% of the rent charged for short-term lodging. The tax
applies to hotels, motels, inns, vacation rentals, campgrounds, recreational vehicle
parks, and other lodging accommodations located in the unincorporated areas of the
County. The tax generally applies to stays of 30 days or less and is paid by the transient
occupant, although it is collected and remitted by the lodging operator or, in some
circumstances, an online booking service.
The measure would increase the existing tax rate by seven percentage points.
According to the ballot question, the increase is estimated to generate approximately
$58,500 in additional annual revenue. The ordinance provides that the tax is a general
tax, meaning the revenue would be deposited into the County's General Fund and may
be used for any lawful governmental purpose, including essential public services, as
determined through the County's annual budget process.
The measure also updates and revises various provisions of the existing Transient
Occupancy Tax ordinance, including definitions and administrative provisions relating to
the collection and enforcement of the tax. These amendments include updating and
clarifying definitions, expressly addressing online booking services, expanding and
clarifying the types of lodging and charges subject to the tax, and making other
revisions intended to clarify the administration, collection, enforcement, and operation of
the ordinance without materially changing its existing framework.
If approved by a majority of voters, the ordinance would become effective on January 1,
2027. The increased tax would remain in effect unless repealed or amended by the
Solano County Board of Supervisors or by the voters. If the measure is not approved,
the County's Transient Occupancy Tax would remain at 5%.
Respectfully submitted,


Carrie Blacklock
Solano County Counsel

measures.questionText: Shall the existing three-quarter (3/4%) percent transactions and use tax measure to support the City of Rio Vista’s general services, including police, fire, parks, and other unrestricted general fund expenditures, be extended for three years, commencing on April 1, 2027, and which is projected to provide between $1,398,000 to $1,467,000 of revenue annually for the City?
measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE O:
RIO VISTA TRANSACTION AND USE TAX MEASURE

The City Council of the City of Rio Vista has placed Measure O on the November 3, 2026 ballot.
California Revenue and Taxation Code section 7285.9 authorizes the City Council to levy a
transactions and use tax by ordinance, provided the ordinance establishing the tax is ultimately
approved by the voters.

If approved by Rio Vista voters, Measure O will impose a three-quarter percent (0.75%)
transactions and use ("sales") tax for three years.

This tax is administered by the California Department of Tax and Fee Administration. Once
established, it is allocated to the city where any goods are delivered or placed into use. Asa
“general tax,” the revenue generated by Measure O will be deposited in the City’s general fund.

Because this tax will be a general tax, the City of Rio Vista will be able to use the tax proceeds
for any legal governmental purpose, including police, fire, parks, and other unrestricted general
fund expenditures. Also, because Measure O is a general tax, it will be approved if over a
majority of voters (over 50%) vote in favor of it. If adopted, Measure O would generate between
$1,398,000 and $1,467,000 annually.

If approved, Measure O would become effective April 1, 2027 and remain in effect until April
2030. The tax would expire at the end of the three-year period unless it is reauthorized by a
majority of the voters at a future election that occurs prior to the expiration of the tax.

A “YES” vote is a vote to approve the 0.75% percent sales tax for a period of three years. A
“NO” vote is a vote against the sales tax.

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure O. If you desire a copy of the ordinance

or measure, please call the elections official's office at (707) 374-6451 and a copy will be mailed
at no cost to you.

Mona G. Ebrahimi, City Attorney

measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE P


If approved by the voters, Measure P would adopt a local Transactions and Use Tax Ordinance
(the “Sales Tax Ordinance”). Measure P would increase the City’s existing sales tax rate by 1%,
or 1 cent, on every dollar of taxable sales of goods in the City, and on the taxable storage, use or
consumption in the City of goods purchased. Measure P would also extend the City’s existing 1%
transactions and use tax until ended by the voters.

The Measure would be a general tax, which means the tax revenue could be spent for all general
governmental purposes. The City estimated that this Measure will raise approximately $24 million
per year in new local revenue for use in the City. The City Council’s adopted ballot question states
this new revenue would be used for general City services including police, fire, 911 emergency
response, neighborhood safety, street and sidewalk repair, and homelessness prevention and
response. The Sales Tax Ordinance would be in effect until ended by the voters. Measure P was
placed on the ballot by a unanimous vote of the City Council.

The revenue generated by the Measure will be collected by the State of California under a contract
with the City, and the revenue will be paid over to the City. Accountability over revenue and
expenditures from the Sales Tax Ordinance will be provided through the City’s budget process
and annual independent audit, which are available to the public. Financial information also is
disclosed in the City’s Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and other public documents. The
total sales tax rate paid in Fairfield, which includes the sales tax collected for the State of
California, Solano County, and other public agencies, is currently 8.375%. If the Measure is
approved by the voters, the total sales tax rate paid in the City would be 9.375%, subject to any
changes in state law. Sales tax is not collected on items such as prescription medications or food
bought as groceries.

Article XIIIC of the California Constitution, commonly known as Proposition 218, requires that
the proposed general tax be approved by a majority of the voters voting on the Measure. A “yes”
vote on Measure P is to adopt the Sales Tax Ordinance. A “no” vote on Measure P is to not
adopt the Sales Tax Ordinance.


David G. Lim
Fairfield City Attorney

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure P. If you desire a complete copy
of the Sales Tax Ordinance, please call the City Clerk at (707) 428-7384 and a copy will be
sent to you at no cost.

measures.questionText: Shall the Office of City Clerk be appointive?
measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE Q
        The proposed Measure seeks to convert the position of Fairfield City Clerk from an
elective to an appointive office.

        The City Clerk is responsible for overseeing vital municipal functions. In the City of
Fairfield, the City Clerk is currently elected to serve a four-year term. The City Council has
directed that Measure Q be placed on the ballot to provide an opportunity for voters to decide
whether the City Clerk should instead be an appointed position. A majority of California
cities have an appointed City Clerk who is either hired by the City Manager or appointed by
the City Council. This Measure allows the City Council to delegate its appointment authority
to the City Manager.

        This Measure will have no impact upon the current term of the incumbent City Clerk.
The incumbent City Clerk was last elected in 2024 and would be permitted to stay in office
until the end of her current term in 2028. At the conclusion of her term, the incumbent City
Clerk would be eligible for appointment to the same office. If the incumbent City Clerk
resigns before the end of her term, a replacement would also be appointed. An appointed City
Clerk would not be required to be a resident or elector of the City, and will receive
compensation in a fixed amount established by the City Council.

        This Measure was placed on the ballot by the Fairfield City Council and requires
the approval of a majority of voters. A “yes” vote on this Measure amends Chapter 2 of
the City Municipal Code in order to make the City Clerk position appointive, meaning no
one will have to run for office for the City Clerk position. A “no” vote on this Measure
means the City Clerk position will remain elected.

        The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure Q. If you desire
copies of the Measure and the proposed Municipal Code amendment, please call the
City Clerk's office at (707) 428-7384, and copies will be mailed at no cost to you.
Copies can also be obtained from the City Clerk’s office at City Hall, 1000 Webster
Street, Fairfield, CA 94533, or the City’s website at https://www.fairfield.ca.gov/.




                                                      _________________________
                                                      David Lim
                                                      City Attorney
                                                      City of Fairfield

measures.officialStatement:
IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE U
                          DIXON UNIFIED SCHOOL DISTRICT
                      GENERAL OBLIGATION BOND MEASURE

Measure U was placed on the ballot by the Governing Board of the Dixon Unified
School District. If approved, Measure U would authorize the District to issue and sell
general obligation bonds in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $49,000,000,
at interest rates within legal limits.

Bond proceeds would be used for school facility projects identified in the measure,
including constructing and renovating classrooms and other school facilities; replacing
deteriorating portable classrooms; repairing or replacing roofs, plumbing, sewer and gas
lines, heating, ventilation, air-conditioning and electrical systems; making health, safety
and seismic improvements; improving technology infrastructure; and constructing or
renovating libraries, multipurpose rooms, cafeterias, athletic facilities, playgrounds and
other school facilities. The District would determine the priority and timing of projects,
and approval of the measure does not guarantee that all listed projects will be
completed.

The measure includes accountability requirements governing the use of bond proceeds.
Bond proceeds may be used only for the purposes specified in the measure and may
not be used for teacher or administrator salaries or other school operating expenses.
The measure requires an independent citizens’ oversight committee, annual
independent performance and financial audits, and annual reports regarding the receipt
and expenditure of bond proceeds and the status of funded projects.

Principal and interest on the bonds would be paid by property taxes levied on taxable
property within the District. According to the District’s Tax Rate Statement, the estimated
average annual tax rate is $29 per $100,000 of assessed valuation, and the estimated
highest tax rate is $30 per $100,000 of assessed valuation. The District estimates that
taxes will be collected through fiscal year 2061-62 and that total debt service, including
principal and interest, will be approximately $105,000,000. These amounts are
estimates and may vary.

A “yes” vote on Measure U means general obligation bonds totaling up to $49,000,000
may be issued to finance the school facility projects specified in the measure.

A “no” vote on Measure U means the bonds will not be authorized.

Measure U requires approval by at least 55 percent of the votes cast on the measure to
pass.

Respectfully submitted,

Carrie Blacklock
Solano County Counsel

measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE V

On June 23, 2026, the City Council of the City of Vacaville unanimously voted to place
Measure V on the November 3, 2026 statewide general election ballot.

Background
The City's General Fund has a projected deficit of approximately $12 million for the current

fiscal year and has already reduced General Fund expenditures by approximately $9 million
through cost-saving measures, as reflected in the City's adopted budget. The deficit is
projected to continue beyond fiscal year 2026/2027.

Tax Measure
|f approved by a majority of the voters voting on the measure, this measure would add

Chapter 3.15 to the Vacavilte Municipal Code, authorizing the City to impose a new
transactions and use tax, commonly referred to as a “sales tax”, of ane percent (1%) on the
sale and use of tangible personal property within the City.

The City's current combined sales tax rate is 8.125% of which the City retains 1.75% of the
revenue generated, with the remaining 6.375% going to the State, Solano County, and the
Solano County Library. If approved Measure V would increase the combined rate to 9.125%,
increasing the City’s share to 2.75%. Revenue from this new tax would be collected and
retained entirely by the City and would not be subject to reallocation by the county, state, or
federal government.

This tax would be administered and collected on the City's behalf by the California
Department of Tax and Fee Administration. With some exceptions, the tax would apply to
tangible products purchased by residents and visitors to the City, such as clothing and
household items. It would not apply to certain sales, including most food products and
prescription medicine.

This tax would be separate from, and in addition to, the City's existing three-quarter percent
(.75%) sales tax, “Measure M”; approval would not modify, reduce, or repeal that tax. The tax
generally follows the same rules, exemptions, and procedures as the existing state sales and
use tax, with certain exceptions specified in the ordinance.

Hf approved, the one-cent sales tax would take effect April 1, 2027. The tax would not expire
on a fixed date and would remain in effect until repealed by a future vote of the City's

qualified voters.

Use of Proceeds

 
This is a local general tax. If approved, revenue would be deposited into the City's General
Fund and could be spent on any lawful municipal purpose at the City Council's discretion,
without legal restriction to any specific purpose or program. The ordinance would establish
a Citizens Oversight Committee to review and annually report to the Council on receipt and
expenditure of the revenue and would require periodic independent audits.

A “yes” vote approves the additional one percent sales tax described above. A “no” vote
rejects it. This measure requires a simple majority of “yes” votes for the measure to pass and

— | tee

Andria Borba, City Attorney

The above statement is an impartial analysis of Measure V. If you desire a copy of the
ordinance or measure, please call the City of Vacaville City Clerk’s Office at 707-449-
5110 and a copy will be mailed to you at no cost.

measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS MEASURE X

Like other California cities, the City of Benicia (City) requires that, generally, any person or entity
conducting business in the City pay a business license tax (BLT) to the City. It is not a tax on
residents, consumers, or users who are not business owners or operators. The Benicia City
Council has placed a Measure on the November 3, 2026 ballot, asking voters to adopt an
ordinance to amend Chapters 5.04 and 5.06 of the Benicia Municipal Code.


For most businesses, the City's current BLT is the sum of three components: a personnel tax of
$7.50 per person employed or compensated (prorated below 2,000 hours); a multifamily
residential rental tax of $36.00 per rental unit, with exemptions for small buildings and units
occupied by seniors or lower-income households; and a gross receipts tax at tiered rates of
$0.75, $0.65, or $0.55 per $1,000 depending on business type, subject to per-business
minimums and a $450.00 annual maximum. Solicitors, farmer's market vendors, and fair
participants instead pay a flat $15.00 alternate tax. Other than the rates on gross receipts which
are fixed under the current ordinance, these dollar amounts are adjusted annually for inflation.


Effective January 1, 2027 the proposed ordinance would tax gross receipts at the following
annual BLT rates, applied per $1,000 of gross receipts:


   •   $0.25 per $1,000 for General and Retail businesses.
   •   $0.75 per $1,000 for Contractors.
   •   $0.75 per $1,000 for Services businesses.
   •   $1.00 per $1,000 for Industrial businesses.
   •   $1.00 per $1,000 for Professional businesses.
   •   $1.00 per $1,000 for Property Rental businesses.
   •   $1.25 per $1,000 for Petroleum businesses


Under the proposed ordinance, each business with less than $100,000 in gross receipts would
be exempt from the BLT, and each business would have an annual maximum license tax of
$25,000. The maximum license tax would be initially set at $1,500, and increased 10% each
year until reaching $25,000 per year. The proposed ordinance also establishes a separate BLT
on marine terminal businesses in the City at a rate of 3 percent of gross receipts, and the
marine terminal tax is not subject to the maximum license tax. First-year revenue under this
structure is estimated to be approximately $1,612,000.
 The BLT is a general tax since the revenue will continue to be placed in the City’s General Fund
and may be used for any general municipal purposes. Therefore, Measure X will not be effective
in amending the BLT until approved by a majority of City voters voting in the election.


A “yes” vote is a vote in favor of the tax.


A “no” vote is a vote against the tax.


Submitted August 11, 2026


Benjamin Stock
City Attorney

provenance.quote: Shall the City of Benicia adopt a Business License Tax measure, exempting businesses with $100,000 or less in annual receipts, setting tax rates by business category ranging from $0.25 to $1.25 per $1,000 in receipts, capping those annual taxes at $1,500 in the first year with 10% annual increases until the cap is $25,000, with a separate Marine Terminal rate of $3 per $100 in receipts, generating approximately $1,612,000 in the first year, until repealed by voters?

measures.questionText: Shall the measure, adopting a limited City Charter for the City of Benicia that allows the real property transfer tax in Measure Z to take effect if voters approve both Measures Y and Z, and continues the City’s existing council-manager form of government, be adopted?
measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE Y

Measure Y asks voters to adopt the City of Benicia Charter (“Charter”) which will allow the City
of Benicia (“City”) to exercise the authority over municipal affairs granted to charter cities by the
California Constitution. The proposed Charter specifically limits the City’s new power over
municipal affairs solely with respect to the power to enact a system for the imposition, levy and
collection of a tax on the conveyance of real property. Accordingly, the proposed Charter allows
the City to enact a Real Property Transfer Tax Ordinance (“Measure Z”), the proceeds of which
will fund City services.

The City is currently a general law city which means the powers of the City are governed by the
general laws established by the State Legislature or enacted by voter initiative. Charter cities,
on the other hand, are specifically authorized by the State Constitution to govern themselves as
to those matters deemed “municipal affairs”. In contrast, state law applies to charter cities for
matters of “statewide concern”.

Whether a given activity is a municipal affair, over which a charter city has sole authority, or of
statewide concern, over which the State legislature has authority, is an issue for the State
judicial system to decide based on the facts and circumstances of each case. Generally, a
matter is of statewide concern rather than a municipal affair when its impact is primarily
regional.

A general law city may elect to become a charter city by following statutory procedures and may
limit the scope of matters the charter governs. Here, the City utilized the procedure in
Government Code section 34458.

A “yes” vote on Measure Y adopts the City of Benicia Charter. A “no” vote on Measure Y will
maintain the City of Benicia as a general law city. Measure Y will be adopted if it is approved by
a majority vote of the electorate. If Measure Y is approved by a majority of voters and the
Charter is adopted, any future amendment or expansion of the scope of the Charter would be
subject to voter approval.

Pursuant to Government Code section 34458.5 requirement for providing certain disclosures in
a ballot description, the proposed Charter specifically limits the City’s new power over municipal
affairs solely with respect to the power to enact a system for the imposition, levy and collection
of a tax on the conveyance of real property, and provides that in all other respects, the powers
of the City shall remain as they currently are, and shall be governed by the general laws of the
State of California. The City’s existing council-manager form of government would continue
unless changed by the voters, and the proposed Charter does not give the City Council any new
powers to raise its compensation or that of other City officials without voter approval.

Measure Y was placed on the ballot by the City Council of the City of Benicia.


Submitted August 11, 2026.


Benjamin Stock
City Attorney

measures.questionText: Shall the Measure, to primarily ensure newly constructed property sales contribute to maintaining city services and infrastructure, establish a real property transfer tax that will not apply to existing homes that sell for $2 million or less, but apply to other property sales at rates of 0.004 for sales $2,000,000 or less, 0.006 for sales $2,000,001 - $10,000,000, and 0.008 for sales over $10,000,000, providing approximately $230,000 annually, until ended by voters, be adopted?
measures.officialStatement:
CITY ATTORNEY’S IMPARTIAL ANALYSIS OF MEASURE Z

Measure Z asks the electorate of the City of Benicia (“City”) to consider the adoption of the City
of Benicia Real Property Transfer Tax Ordinance (“Ordinance”). A companion measure,
Measure Y, is also being presented on the November 3, 2026, ballot. Measure Y, if approved,
would adopt the City of Benicia Charter which gives the City new power over municipal affairs to
enact a system for the imposition, levy and collection of a real property transfer tax. The
adoption of the Charter is legally necessary to allow the City to enact a real property transfer tax
which is a tax imposed when real property is sold. Measure Z can only be approved if the voters
approve Measure Y.

Because this measure does not legally restrict the use of tax revenue to any specific purposes,
it is classified as a “general tax,” not a “special tax.” As a general tax, the funds would go to the
City's general fund, and be used for any valid municipal government purpose including roads,
infrastructure, facilities, Police, Fire, and other City services.

The City is currently a general law city, governed by the laws of the State of California relating to
general law cities. One of those general laws, California Revenue and Taxation Code Section
11911, authorized the City’s current real property transfer tax rate of $0.275 for each $500.00 or
fractional part of $500.00. If Measure Y passes, the City will have the authority to impose a real
property transfer tax that exceeds the tax rates in the City’s current ordinance, conditioned on
Measure Z also passing.

If adopted, the Ordinance would establish a new local tax on the conveyance of real property as
follows:


•   Sales $2,000,000 or less: $4 per $1000

•   Sales over $2,000,000 and up to $10,000,000: $6 per $1,000

•   Sales over $10,000,000: $8 per $1,000


The Ordinance contains certain exemptions, including sales of residential homes built before
January 1, 2027 and that sells for $2,000,000 or less. The Ordinance further allows buyers and
sellers to negotiate among themselves as to who pays the tax.

The tax is estimated to generate approximately $230,000 annually, growing to between $3.3
million and $3.8 million by 2050.

A “yes” vote on Measure Z adopts the Ordinance. A “no” vote on Measure Z rejects the
Ordinance; however, the current tax authorized by California Revenue and Taxation Code
Section 11911 would remain in effect. Measure Z will be adopted and the Ordinance will
become effective only if both Measure Y and Z are approved by a majority vote.

Measure Z was placed on the ballot by the City Council of the City of Benicia.

Submitted August 11, 2026.

Benjamin Stock

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorize up to $29.9 million in school-facility bonds for repairs, classroom upgrades, safety, accessibility, technology and other listed projects. Property taxes would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $1.6 million annually, an average rate of $46 and highest rate of $49 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2061–62, and $58.6 million total repayment. These are estimates, not binding caps, and actual rates and repayment could differ. State law allows issuance only within its projected $60-per-$100,000 tax-rate limit. Funds could not pay teacher or administrator salaries, pensions or other operating expenses. A separate account, independent citizen oversight, annual performance and financial audits and annual reports are required. Completion of all projects is not guaranteed and may depend on state matching funds. Approval requires 55% of votes.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize the district to issue up to $29.9 million in bonds and levy property taxes to repay them under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds or their repayment property tax through this measure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Change business-license taxes on specified facilities in unincorporated Solano County, outside cities, starting January 1, 2027. Raise the wind-generation tax from $0.00003 to $0.00008 per kilowatt-hour and add taxes on commercial solar generation, grid-connected battery storage, natural-gas extraction and data centers at the rates below. From January 1, 2028, rates would increase annually with the specified consumer-price index and could not decrease. Federal and state tax exemptions would remain. Estimated additional revenue is $353,000 annually for the county general fund, available for any lawful purpose; the ordinance has no fixed expiration. It requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the updated business-license tax categories, rates and annual inflation adjustments.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the current business-license provisions, including the existing wind-turbine rate, without the new categories or annual inflation adjustments.

parts.label: Facility tax rates
parts.what: Commercial solar generation would pay $0.00008 per kilowatt-hour. Front-of-the-meter battery storage would pay $1.50 per month per megawatt-hour of approved storage capacity, regardless of actual charging or discharging. Natural-gas extraction would pay $0.30 per thousand cubic feet. Data centers would pay $5 annually per square foot of gross floor area, including associated equipment-pad areas for supporting behind-the-meter batteries and natural-gas turbines.

parts.label: Covered facilities and exemptions
parts.what: Wind, solar and natural-gas facilities are covered when primarily producing for resale or off-site use. Grid-connected batteries primarily serving wholesale grid functions are covered. Data centers serve off-site users; computer and IT infrastructure accessory to and primarily supporting an on-site business, government, agricultural, industrial or institutional use is excluded. Federal and state business-tax exemptions remain.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase the lodging tax in unincorporated Solano County, outside cities, from 5% to 12% of taxable rent starting January 1, 2027. It generally applies to stays of 30 days or less at hotels, motels, vacation rentals, campgrounds, RV parks and other covered lodging. Guests pay the tax, collected by operators or applicable online booking services. The ordinance updates definitions, taxable charges, collection and enforcement rules while retaining the exemptions described below. The county estimates $58,500 in additional annual revenue for any lawful general-fund purpose. There is no fixed expiration date; the official analysis says the supervisors or voters could repeal or amend it. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the 12% lodging-tax rate and ordinance updates.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the current 5% county lodging-tax rate.

parts.label: Lodging and charges
parts.what: Covered lodging includes vacation rentals, RV parks and seasonal or event-based public or private campgrounds. Hospital, clinic and care-home rooms, local-government lodging, state-park campsites and legally defined organized camps are excluded. Taxable rent includes required lodging fees and specified related charges; separately itemized optional services listed in the ordinance are excluded.

parts.label: Guest exemptions
parts.what: Exemptions include qualifying official government or federal-credit-union travel with the required certificate and direct official payment; nonprofit-voucher emergency housing during a disaster; free promotional rooms without non-cash payment other than advertising; and eligible timeshare or membership-campsite owners and guests accompanying them.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Extend Rio Vista’s existing 0.75% sales and use tax for three years, from April 1, 2027 through March 31, 2030. Estimated revenue is $1,398,000–$1,467,000 annually. It would go to the general fund for any lawful city purpose, including police, fire, parks and other services. The tax would expire after the three-year period unless a future majority vote renews it before expiration. This measure also requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Extend the 0.75% sales and use tax for this three-year period.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not extend the existing tax for this additional three-year period.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Increase Fairfield’s local sales and use tax from 1% to 2% and remove its scheduled March 31, 2033 expiration, continuing it until ended by voters. The current combined sales-tax rate would rise from 8.375% to 9.375%, subject to changes in state law. Most groceries and prescription medicines remain exempt. The city estimates $24 million in new annual revenue for any general city purpose, including public safety, streets and homelessness services. Independent citizen oversight, annual audits and public spending reports are specified. If the full 1-percentage-point increase is found invalid, the council could reduce the increase to 0.875 percentage points, for a 1.875% city tax. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the extension and increase of the local sales and use tax, subject to the stated fallback if the full increase is invalid.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not approve this extension and increase; the existing tax ordinance would remain in place.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Make Fairfield’s city clerk appointed rather than elected. The council would appoint the clerk, who would serve at its pleasure, and could delegate appointment to the city manager by ordinance. The appointee would not have to be a city resident or registered voter; the council would set compensation. The current elected clerk’s term through 2028 would remain intact unless she leaves early. Appointment would begin when that term ends or an earlier vacancy occurs, and the incumbent could be appointed. The council could later amend the ordinance, but restoring an elected clerk would require voter approval. This measure requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Make the city clerk an appointed office under these transition rules.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep the city clerk elected to four-year terms.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Authorize up to $49 million in school-facility bonds for classroom, infrastructure, health, safety, seismic, technology and other listed projects. Property taxes would repay principal and interest. The district estimates $3 million annually, an average rate of $29 and highest rate of $30 per $100,000 of assessed value, collection through fiscal year 2061–62, and approximately $105 million total repayment. These estimates may vary and are not binding maximums. Interest rates must stay within legal limits. Funds could not pay teacher or administrator salaries or other operating expenses. Independent citizen oversight, annual financial and performance audits and annual reports are required. The district would set project priorities and timing; approval does not guarantee every listed project will be completed. Approval requires 55% of votes.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Authorize the district to issue up to $49 million in bonds and levy property taxes to repay them under these conditions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Do not authorize these bonds through this measure.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Add a 1% sales and use tax beginning April 1, 2027, increasing Vacaville’s current combined rate from 8.125% to 9.125%. It would remain until repealed by voters. This would be separate from the existing 0.75% Measure M tax, which would stay unchanged. Most food products and prescription medicine would remain exempt. The city estimates $28 million annually, locally retained in the general fund for any lawful city purpose at council discretion. Annual audits and public reporting would be required. A Citizens Oversight Committee would review revenue and spending and report annually. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the additional 1% sales and use tax and its accountability provisions.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this additional tax; existing taxes would remain unchanged.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Set a new Benicia business-license tax schedule beginning January 1, 2027, based on annual gross receipts and business category. Businesses with $100,000 or less in receipts would be exempt. Other businesses would pay the rates below, with a $1,500 first-year annual cap that rises 10% each January 1 starting in 2028 until it reaches $25,000. Marine terminals would instead pay 3% of gross receipts without that cap. Estimated first-year revenue is $1,612,000 for the general fund, available for any lawful city purpose, until repealed by voters. The council could lower or suspend the tax and restore it within authorized limits; increases beyond the authorized amounts would need voters. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Approve the new business-license tax rates, exemptions and phased cap.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject this new tax schedule and keep the current business-license tax rules.

parts.label: Rates by business category
parts.what: Per $1,000 in gross receipts, general and retail businesses would pay $0.25; contractors and services $0.75; industrial, professional and property-rental businesses $1; and petroleum businesses $1.25. Marine terminals would pay $3 per $100, or 3%, without the annual cap.

parts.label: Other exemptions
parts.what: Constitutional and state-law exemptions remain. Additional exemptions cover qualifying honorably discharged disabled veterans unable to earn a living through manual labor, and federally recognized 501(c)(3) organizations except for business activities subject to federal income tax.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Adopt a limited Benicia charter giving the city new authority solely to levy and administer a tax on real-property transfers, beyond the amount permitted for general-law cities. The separate Measure Z tax could take effect only if voters approve both Y and Z. The charter itself would preserve the current council-manager government and leave other city powers under the state’s general laws. It would give the council no new power to raise its own or other officials’ compensation without voter approval. Future charter amendments or expanded authority would also require a majority vote. Existing rights, liabilities, ordinances and legal proceedings would continue. Approval requires a majority vote.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Adopt the limited charter; the proposed transfer tax would still require Measure Z to pass.
measureRecords.noMeans: Keep Benicia a general-law city; the proposed Measure Z tax could not take effect.

measureRecords.whatItDoes: Create an additional Benicia real-property transfer tax only if both this measure and the limited charter in Measure Y receive majority approval. It would apply to transfers valued above $100 after excluding encumbrances that remain on the property. For each $1,000 or fraction of taxable value, the rate would be $4 for sales up to $2 million, $6 for sales above $2 million through $10 million, and $8 for sales above $10 million. Residential improvements substantially completed before January 1, 2027 would be exempt when the sale does not exceed $2 million. Other exemptions are described below. Buyers and sellers would be jointly responsible but could agree how to split the tax. Estimated revenue is $230,000 annually, growing to $3.3–$3.8 million by 2050, for any lawful general-fund purpose. Annual audits and a Citizens Oversight Committee would be required. The tax would continue until ended by voters.
measureRecords.yesMeans: Adopt the additional transfer tax and its exemptions, if Measure Y also passes.
measureRecords.noMeans: Reject the additional transfer tax; the existing state-authorized transfer tax would remain in effect.

parts.label: Home, family and affordable-housing exemptions
parts.what: Transfers among parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, siblings, and spouses or domestic partners would be exempt, including covered separation or divorce settlements. The definition of children includes sons- and daughters-in-law, stepchildren, and children adopted before age 18. Affordable housing would be exempt with a recorded, enforceable city covenant restricting ownership and occupancy to low- or moderate-income households for at least 30 years after transfer. Existing residential improvements substantially completed before January 1, 2027 would be exempt at sale values of $2 million or less.

parts.label: Other qualifying transfers
parts.what: Exemptions cover instruments securing debt, government agencies acquiring title, and specified reorganizations or identity changes filed within five years. Qualifying SEC-ordered conveyances and transfers of interests in continuing partnerships that keep the property are exempt. Foreclosure transfers to a lender are exempt only up to the unpaid debt, accrued interest and foreclosure cost; consideration above that remains taxable.
